name: Paid height growth courses

lead: Paid height growth courses are digital guides, PDFs or coaching packages that claim to add height, including for adults whose growth plates are closed. Buyers hope for a taller standing frame, one of the most sought-after changes in looksmaxxing.

In forum threads, sellers describe methods such as peptide protocols, bone 'microfracture' stimulus routines and sleep-time stretching, and share before-and-after claims. Reference sources on growth describe growth plates fusing in the mid to late teens, and no published trial has tested these courses. Forum members frequently question the claims in the same threads.

paras: Courses are usually sold as PDFs or videos, sometimes shared on forums by buyers who then ask whether the claims are real. The contents described in threads range from nutrition and sleep to stretching routines, loaded leg exercises and injected compounds. Results are typically reported as gains of a centimetre or a few over weeks or months, measured by the buyer.

Financial loss is the most direct risk. Threads describe routines involving heavy loading to induce bone stress and injected research peptides, which carry injury, infection and unregulated-product risks. Clinicians point to a daily height variation of around 1.5 cm in children, which can make measured gains look larger than they are. Medical advice for concerns about growth is to consult an endocrinologist.

lead: Paid height growth courses are commercial guides sold to people who want to be taller. They appear as PDFs, video programmes or coaching offers and often target adults, a group for whom standard medical references describe growth as finished. The pitch is a taller body without surgery, and in some cases a lower-cost alternative to limb lengthening surgery.

Descriptions on looksmax.org vary. One thread shows a buyer asking whether a course author's reported gain from 5'7" to 5'10" after plate closure is genuine; the course text, as quoted, describes injected IGF-1 analogs delivered around the bone, and a reply calls the wording 'buzzword soup' [1]. Another thread offers a 23-page PDF on a 'microfractures technique' said to have been written by someone who grew 8 cm at 21 [2].

Reference sources describe growth plates fusing from about 12 in girls to as late as 17 in boys [3], and describe adult height as strongly influenced by genetics, with twin studies putting heritability at 60 to 80 percent [4]. No published trial has evaluated a commercial height course.

paras: The courses are information products. Threads on looksmax.org describe PDFs of a few dozen pages, larger video collections, and offers shared by users who bought them and relay or resell the contents [2]. A buyer in one thread described a recently purchased course and asked whether the seller's reported height gain was legitimate [1].

Claims quoted in forum threads include stimulating bone with peptide analogs placed near the bone, creating 'microfractures' through loaded or impact exercise followed by high protein and rest, and overnight stretching [1][2]. Sellers present reported gains such as 1 cm in two months or several centimetres over a longer span, sometimes with photographs.

Proponents argue that a stimulus plus nutrition and hormones can regrow or add bone even when growth plates have closed. They compare their approach to surgical limb lengthening, in which bone is deliberately fractured and gradually lengthened.

Reference sources describe plate fusion between about 14 and 17 in most boys, after which the plate is replaced by a line and the bone no longer lengthens at that site [3]. Adult height is described as strongly genetic, with nutrition and health as modifiers [4]. Males usually stop growing around 18 or 19 [4].

Height varies through the day; one study found children lost on average 1.54 cm between getting out of bed and the late afternoon, and measurement error of 0.5 cm can hide or exaggerate real short-term change [4]. Researchers cite such variation when interpreting self-reported gains.
No studies found. Registered clinical trials in the area concern growth hormone treatment in children with medical conditions, not commercial courses.

Forum participants themselves raise doubts about specific courses, and some threads describe the methods in terms of injected research peptides or repeated bone loading. These carry the usual risks of unregulated compounds and overloaded joints. Cost is a further consideration for buyers.

Height is a central concern in looksmaxxing, and courses circulate because many members seek alternatives to expensive surgery. Threads mix hopeful buyers, sellers, and sceptics who ask for photos, measurement methods and independent verification.

lore.intro: Course sellers and buyers on looksmax.org present height growth after plate closure as achievable, while many replies question the evidence and ask for proof.
